The finite counting service budget and baseline bound

This proof supplies the service budget and baseline estimate used in the counting extremizer theorem. All counts exclude the label zero. The parameter alpha is fixed before any limit is taken.

Let beta_star be the unique zero on [2/5,1/2] of

P(b) = 1+9b-2b^2-42b^3-19b^4+20b^5+7b^6-8b^7+2b^8.

The argument proves liminf A(n)/n <= beta_star and liminf d(n)/n <= 1/(1-beta_star). It does not assume an ordered diagonal inverse or prove convergence. In the proof below the same root is written beta_*.

1. Definitions and established game core

For q>=r>=0, use the complete positive-mex/carry recurrence. Its history and same-row prefix at (q,r) are respectively

H(q,r)={d(a):a<r} union {f(a,r):r<=a<q},
C(q,r)={f(q,b):b<r},      d(q)=f(q,q).

For q>r, if f(q-1,r)<q the value is carried; otherwise the value is the positive mex of H(q,r) union C(q,r). Write D=image(d), S=positive integers outside D, and R(x)=#(D intersect [1,x])=x-A(x).

We use these established facts of the actual game:

  1. d is injective; each row consists of distinct positive values and has maximum d(q)>q. A noncarry value is at least q.
  2. A column's pre-retirement awards are distinct and avoid its inherited diagonal labels. The mex envelope is f(q,r)<=q+r+1.
  3. Each p in S has exactly one victim s(p)<p with f(p,s(p))=p. That column carries permanently afterward. These victims are distinct for distinct p.
  4. Row-start propagation: if f(p,s)=p, then p occurs in a column below s in every row s<q<p.

The canonical foundation (../../audit/full/CANONICAL-FOUNDATIONS.md) derives these inputs from the actual-game definitions and names their exact Lean bridges. In particular, row-start propagation, persistent COPY, positive MEX coverage and diagonal maximality are actual-game facts.

For clarity, the two booker consequences used below follow directly. If p in S and q<p, then p occurs in row q exactly when d(q)>p, by the diagonal mex and row maximality. All R(p) owners of D-labels <=p have index below p, since d(a)>a. Therefore p has precisely p-R(p)=A(p) predeath occurrences. They occupy distinct columns. Every such column is below s(p): for q<s this is automatic, at q=s the diagonal is in D, and for s<q<p use row-start propagation and row injectivity. Call this BOOKER-BELOW. Propagation in the p-s-1 intervening rows further gives p-s-1<=s, hence s(p)>=(p-1)/2.

Enumerate S by p_1<p_2<... and write s_j=s(p_j). Diagonal injectivity and d(q)<=2q+1 imply R(x)>=ceil(x/2), so A(x)<=floor(x/2) and p_j>=2j.

2. The upper service budget retains the full excess area

Let G(N) be the number of physical nonbirth D-service cells in rows q<N. Every S-label below d(q) occurs in row q by diagonal mex, and no greater label occurs by maximality. Removing the single diagonal birth gives

G(N)=sum_(q<N)[q-A(d(q))].                                (1)

Fix 0<alpha<1/2 and C>=0 with A(x)>=alphax-C for all nonnegative x. Put lambda=1-alpha and E(x)=A(x)-alphax+C>=0. Constants in O(N) below may depend on this fixed alpha,C, but never on N.

Let b_j be the jth smallest element of the SET D, indexed from j=1. The first N emitted diagonal labels form an N-element subset of D; sorting this subset and using monotonicity of A gives

sum_(q<N) A(d(q)) >= sum_(j=1)^N A(b_j)
                 =sum_(j=1)^N (b_j-j).

Thus G(N)<=N^2-sum b_j. The layer-cake identity is exact:

sum_(j=1)^N b_j=sum_(x>=0)(N-R(x))_+.

For sufficiently large N put B=floor((N-C)/lambda). For 0<=x<=B, N-R(x)=N-C-lambda*x+E(x)>=0. Keeping these terms yields

G(N)<=U_N-sum_(x=0)^B E(x),                              (2)
U_N=N^2-(B+1)(N-C)+lambda*B(B+1)/2
   =[(1-2alpha)/(2(1-alpha))]N^2+O(N).

The coefficient of the area is exactly one. No order of emitted diagonals has been assumed.

3. Current live histories, and payment for static and birth labels

Let F_N(a) count columns 0<=r<a live at the START of row N. A column retiring at N is included. Put

m=R(N-1),   u=F_N(m),
W=sum_(r<m, r live at N) r.

All m owners with d(a)<N have a<N. Each old live column r<N has a history H(N,r) containing N distinct positive labels: r inherited labels and N-r awards. Its missing labels below N are exactly

{p in S:p<N, s(p)<=r}.                                   (3)

Indeed, a D-label below N cannot occur in the row-N prefix, where sub-N values are carried S-labels, and hence must lie in the history. An S-label with victim at most r was not booked by this live column, by BOOKER-BELOW. For a victim above r, inspect column r in row p: it was live then, and its current service exceeds p, since p occurs later in that row. The mex rule therefore forces p into its history.

Consequently the future-label part Q_r=H(N,r) intersect [N,infinity) has size one plus the number of columns <=r retired before N. If r_i is the ith live column (i=1,2,...), this size is r_i+2-i. The envelope on inherited, birth and later awards gives Q_r subset [N,N+r].

Let FD_r count actual nonbirth D-awards represented in Q_r. Removing possible S-labels and all possible inherited/birth D-labels gives

FD_r>=|Q_r|-[A(N+r)-A(N-1)]-#{a<=r:d(a)>=N}.             (4)

Completed D-labels force a separate count

C_N=sum_(a:d(a)<N) F_N(a).

For each pair (a,r), r<a live at N, mex forces d(a) into the column's history. It is neither inherited nor that column's birth. Distinct pairs give distinct physical nonbirth cells. Their labels are <N, whereas the labels counted by FD_r are >=N; the two counts are disjoint.

On the prefix r<m, the total static/birth subtraction in (4) is

T=sum_(a<m,d(a)>=N)[u-F_N(a)].

There are exactly as many missing completed owners below m as completed owners at or beyond m. Direct expansion gives the exact identity

C_N-T=sum_(a<m)F_N(a)
           +sum_(a>=m,d(a)<N)[F_N(a)-u]
       >=sum_(a<m)F_N(a).                               (5)

This pays the entire subtraction without ordering the diagonal owners.

Sum (4) over the u live columns r<m and use (5). Since their ranks are 1 through u, sum |Q_r|=W+3u/2-u^2/2. Also

sum_(a<m)F_N(a)=(m-1)u-W,
A(N+r)-A(N-1)=alpha(r+1)+E(N+r)-E(N-1).

Combine with (2). If N+m-1<=B, the distinct samples E(N+r) are all terms of its area and cancel with coefficient one. The whole low area remains:

m*u-alpha*W-u^2/2+L_N<=U_N,
L_N=sum_(x=0)^(N-1)E(x).                                (6)

The terms dropped to obtain (6) are nonnegative: (1/2-alpha)u, u*E(N-1), the last surplus in (5), and unsampled high excess area. This is a finite statement about currently live columns, not a limit or an assumption of immortality.

4. Chronologically unusable columns sharpen the victim bound

First s_j<=2j-1: in row p_j every live column before the victim must have booked p_j earlier. The prefix is covered by at most j prebookers and at most j-1 columns already retired.

A column s_i retiring at p_i never awards above p_i+s_i. Before death this follows from the mex envelope; after death its value is p_i. If p_i+s_i<p, it therefore never booked p. Moreover it is below s(p), since

2s_i+1<=p_i+s_i<p,    s(p)>=(p-1)/2.

These unusable columns are distinct from the A(p) booker columns, and both sets lie strictly below the victim. Hence

s(p)>=A(p)+#{i:p_i+s_i<p}.                               (7)

Since i=A(p_i)>=alpha*p_i-C and s_i<=2i-1, p_i+s_i<=(1/alpha+2)i+O(1). Thus (7) implies

s(p)>=A(p)+[alpha/(1+2alpha)]p-O(1).                     (8)

Set h=1+2alpha and g=1+alpha. Using E(p_j)=j-alpha*p_j+C, (8) is equivalently the useful lower constraint

E(p_j)>=2g*j-h*s_j-O(1).                                (9)

All constants here are uniform in the deadline rank.

5. Past retirements force low excess: a first moment and a backward ramp

There are K=m-u already-dead columns below m, with distinct deadline ranks and deadlines p<N. The sum of their physical indices is m(m-1)/2-W. Summing (9), and using a rank sum at least K(K+1)/2, gives for the FULL low S-sample sum

S_N:=sum_(p in S,p<N)E(p) >= B_ret-O(N),
B_ret=h*W+g*(m-u)^2-h*m^2/2.                            (10)

We may pass from the selected subset to the full sum because E>=0.

For a second estimate, suppose K>0 and let J be the largest selected deadline rank. Then J>=K, p_J<N, and s_J<m. Equation (9) gives

E(p_J)>=2g*J-h*m-O(1)>=H-O(1),
H=m-2g*u.                                               (11)

For every j<=J, distinct increasing deadlines obey p_J-p_j>=J-j, so

E(p_J)-E(p_j)=(J-j)-alpha*(p_J-p_j)
               <=(1-alpha)(J-j).                        (12)

Thus a high excess at p_J forces a backward ramp through all preceding S-ranks, including ranks whose victims were not selected. Its width fits inside ranks 1 through J up to O(1), because p_J>=J implies E(p_J)<=(1-alpha)J+C. Summing the nonnegative ramp gives

S_N>=B_peak-O(N),
B_peak=(m-2g*u)_+^2/[2(1-alpha)].                        (13)

The discrete triangular-sum and initial-boundary errors are O(N), for fixed alpha,C; replacing E(p_J) by H-O(1) has the same error size. If K=0, then H<=0, so (13) follows from S_N>=0 without defining J.

The two estimates concern the SAME mass. Therefore we take their maximum, not their sum. For t>=1, Delta E(t)=1_S(t)-alpha. The exact square identity is

S_N=alpha*sum_(t=1)^(N-1)E(t)
     +[E(N-1)^2-E(0)^2]/2
     +sum_(t=1)^(N-1)(Delta E(t))^2/2.                  (14)

It follows by summing 2E(t)Delta E(t)=E(t)^2-E(t-1)^2+(Delta E(t))^2. The last sum is O(N). Combining (10),(13),(14) therefore yields

L_N>=max(B_ret,B_peak)/alpha
           -E(N-1)^2/(2alpha)-O(N).                    (15)

The endpoint square is retained. All these samples have p<N and were not used in cancelling the high samples N+r in Section 3.

6. Joint optimization of the finite inequality

For m>0 put v=u/m and z=W/m^2. Apart from the endpoint cost in (15), the normalized left side of (6) is bounded below by

v-v^2/2-alpha*z
  +max(h*z+g*(1-v)^2-h/2,
        (1-2g*v)_+^2/[2(1-alpha)])/alpha.               (16)

Minimizing over every real z enlarges the physical feasible set and is a valid lower relaxation. The z-slope is -alpha below the crossing of the two branches and h/alpha-alpha>0 above it. At the crossing (16) is

J_alpha(v)=alpha/(2h)+k*(v-v^2/2)
                      +w*(1-2g*v)_+^2/2,
k=(1-2alpha^2)/h,
w=(h-alpha^2)/(alpha*h*(1-alpha)).                       (17)

For 2/5<=alpha<1/2, k,w>0. On v>=1/(2g), J is nondecreasing since its derivative is k(1-v). Below that breakpoint J is strictly convex, with vertex

v_*=(2g*w-k)/(4g^2*w-k).

This is positive, since 2g(h-alpha^2)>alpha(1-alpha)(1-2alpha^2), and v_*<1/(2g) follows from (2g-1)k>0. The global minimum on 0<=v<=1 is

M(alpha)=[3+7alpha+alpha^2-5alpha^3-2alpha^4+2alpha^5]
           /[2(4+15alpha+17alpha^2+2alpha^3-6alpha^4)]. (18)

The denominator is positive on [2/5,1/2]. Physical first-moment and rank-spacing constraints have been relaxed, not asserted to attain this minimum. Equations (6),(15)--(18) give the finite inequality

U_N >= m^2*M(alpha)-E(N-1)^2/(2alpha)-O(N).               (19)

7. Fixed-parameter limit order, root, and diagonal transfer

Let beta=liminf A(N)/N<=1/2. If beta<=2/5, the baseline density conclusion is automatic. Otherwise fix 2/5<alpha<beta. A finite global C as used above exists by the definition of liminf. Choose a subsequence A(N)/N -> beta. Then

m/N -> 1-beta,   B/N -> 1/(1-alpha),
E(N-1)/N -> beta-alpha.

The range condition N+m-1<=B eventually holds: 2-beta<8/5 while 1/(1-alpha)>5/3. Divide (19) by N^2 at this FIXED alpha and take the subsequence limit:

(1-2alpha)/(2(1-alpha))
   >=(1-beta)^2*M(alpha)-(beta-alpha)^2/(2alpha).         (20)

Only now let alpha increase to beta. The endpoint cost tends to zero; there is no exchange of limits requiring uniform error constants. With

V(b)=3+7b+b^2-5b^3-2b^4+2b^5,
D0(b)=4+15b+17b^2+2b^3-6b^4,

the resulting necessary inequality is

(1-2beta)D0(beta)-(1-beta)^3 V(beta)=P(beta)>=0.          (21)

On [2/5,1/2],

P'(b)=9-4b-126b^2-76b^3+100b^4+42b^5-56b^6+16b^7
      <=9-4b-95b^2-76b^3-48b^6<0.

Here use 100b^4<=25b^2, 42b^5<=6b^2 and 16b^7<=8b^6. The endpoint signs are positive at 2/5 and negative at 1/2. Exact integer evaluation certifies

.46995152763789 < beta_* < .46995152763790,
1.88661990769183 < 1/(1-beta_*) < 1.88661990769187.

The strict derivative estimate above proves uniqueness. The displayed decimal bracket is verified by substituting its two rational endpoints in P; it is not a floating-point assumption. Therefore (21) implies beta<=beta_*.

Finally, if liminf d(n)/n>c, then d(n)>=cn-O(1), whence injectivity gives R(x)<=x/c+O(1) and liminf A(x)/x>=1-1/c. If the diagonal liminf exceeded 1/(1-beta_), choose c strictly between them to contradict the density bound. This proves the baseline bound without assuming an inverse ordered sequence.
